project.pyy = f · Y / Z

B · Digital Image 🔍 Explore — Bit-depth & File Size

See how bits-per-channel trade quality for size:

explore.py
h, w, c = img.shape
for b in [8, 4, 2, 1]:

Fewer bits → fewer colors and a smaller file. 8-bit gives 256 levels per channel.

C · Color Spaces · 🎛️ Interactive RGB — Three Numbers per Pixel (1/3)
☀ in light 60, 180, 75 H 128° · S 67% · V 71%
🌥 in shade 33, 99, 41 H 127° · S 67% · V 39%
R 60
G 180
B 75

Same colour in both boxes — but all three numbers drop together in shade.

In HSV, H (hue) stays the same — only V (brightness) drops → easier to isolate a colour.

🎨

Every pixel = three numbers (R, G, B), each 0–255

⚠️

Change the lighting and all three shift together — so "green" has no single RGB value. Hard to isolate a colour.

1 / 58
C · Color Spaces The HSV Cylinder (2/3)
✅

HSV separates color (H) from brightness (V)

Selecting “green” = picking one hue range — robust to light & shadow.

①Convert RGB → grayscale (1 channel)
②Convert RGB → HSV

convert.pycv2.cvtColor
import cv2
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY)

C · Color Spaces 🔍 Explore — The Luminosity Weights

Is grayscale just the average of R, G, B?

explore.py
def gray(r, g, b): return round(0.299*r + 0.587*g + 0.114*b)
for rgb in [(255,0,0), (0,255,0), (0,0,255)]:
    print(rgb, "->", gray(*rgb))
🔎

No — green weighs most (0.587), blue least (0.114), matching how the eye perceives brightness.

D · Image Sampling Key Terms — Image Sampling

Spatial sampling

/ˈspeɪ.ʃəl ˈsæm.plɪŋ/

Capturing an image as pixels on a grid.

การสุ่มภาพเป็นพิกเซลบนตาราง

Resolution

/ˌrez.əˈluː.ʃən/

How many pixels make up the image.

จำนวนพิกเซลที่ประกอบเป็นภาพ

Aliasing

/ˈeɪ.li.ə.sɪŋ/

Jagged artifacts from sampling too coarsely.

ขอบหยัก/ลายเพี้ยนจากการสุ่มหยาบเกินไป

Moiré

/mwɑːˈreɪ/

A false pattern when fine detail is sampled too coarsely.

ลายปลอมที่เกิดเมื่อสุ่มรายละเอียดถี่ด้วยพิกเซลน้อยเกินไป

Nyquist rate

/ˈnaɪ.kwɪst/

Sample at > 2× the finest detail — below this, aliasing appears.

ต้องสุ่ม > 2 เท่าของรายละเอียดที่ถี่สุด · ต่ำกว่านี้เกิด aliasing

1 / 58
D · Image Sampling An Image is 2D Sampling
scene + grid
→
sampled pixels
grid 24×24

Each cell → one pixel = the average colour inside it

▦

The scene is continuous, but we store it on a grid.

Each pixel holds the average color of its cell.

Two ways to sample a cell: take the value at one point, or average the whole cell (what cameras do — this widget).

Same idea as 1D sampling in DSP (Digital Signal Processing) — now in 2D.

1 / 58
D · Image Sampling Resolution & Detail

More pixels → more detail, but a bigger file.

Too few pixels → you see the blocks, detail is lost.

⚖️

Trade-off: detail vs storage.

🔬

In research: full detail also needs sampling focus, not just pixels — extended-depth-of-field imaging fuses many focal planes into one all-in-focus microscope capture via pixel-level Gaussian voting.
Extended Depth of Field · NIT Kurume College (exchange research), Japan · 2017

D · Image Sampling Where Aliasing Comes From

Sample fine stripes with a grid that's too coarse…

〰️

…and false patterns (moiré) or jagged edges appear.

Same aliasing as in DSP — here it is spatial.

D · Image Sampling 🔍 Explore — Sweep the Sampling Step

More spacing between samples → fewer pixels:

explore.py
for step in [1, 2, 4, 8, 16]:
    print(f"every {step}: {img.shape[0]//step} x {img.shape[1]//step} px")
🔎

Bigger step → coarser image. To keep detail you must sample finely enough (Nyquist).

Because y∝Z1​ — doubling Z halves the object's height in the image.

❌ Common mistake: confusing linear distance with area — it's not quadratic here.

✎Checkpoint — Digital Image⏱ 3 min

A grayscale image is 1920×1080, 8-bit. How many bytes to store it (uncompressed)?

A) ~2 MB
B) ~6 MB
C) ~2 KB
D) ~16 MB
1 / 58
✔Answer — Digital Image
A) ~2 MB

1920×1080×1=2,073,600 bytes≈2 MB

Grayscale has a single channel, so 8-bit = 1 byte per pixel.

❌ Common mistake: forgetting grayscale = 1 channel; RGB would be ×3 (~6 MB).

Given(R,G,B) = (100, 200, 50)
Step 10.299⋅100+0.587⋅200+0.114⋅50
Step 2=29.9+117.4+5.7
Step 3=153.0≈153
∴ Gray = 153 (G term dominates)

✎Checkpoint — Color Spaces⏱ 3 min

To detect a red ball under changing sunlight, which color space is most robust — and why? (one line)

1 / 58
✔Answer — Color Spaces
HSV

Hue stays stable while brightness (V) changes with sunlight, so a hue range still isolates the ball.

❌ Common mistake: using RGB — all 3 channels shift together when lighting changes.
1 / 58
🧮 Worked Example — Sampling & Aliasing
Givena pattern repeats every 6 mm (period)
Step 1Nyquist: need > 2 pixels across the finest detail → spacing ≤ period ÷ 2
Step 2spacing ≤ 6 ÷ 2 = 3 mm
∴ pixels ≤ 3 mm apart to capture the detail — coarser → a false pattern (moiré / aliasing)
1 / 58
✎Checkpoint — Sampling & Aliasing⏱ 2 min

A striped pattern repeats every 8 mm. To capture it without aliasing, samples must be at most how far apart?

A) 4 mm
B) 8 mm
C) 16 mm
D) 2 mm
1 / 58
✔Answer — Sampling & Aliasing
A) 4 mm

Nyquist for images: you need at least 2 samples per period, so the spacing must be ≤ period ÷ 2 = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 mm. Sampling farther apart misses the stripes and they alias into a false (moiré) pattern.

❌ Common mistake: one sample per period (8 mm) — that's not enough; the stripes disappear or alias.

Topics covered: Image formation · Digital image · Color spaces

📋Case — Traffic Camera

A traffic camera 8 m above a road. Given focal length, sensor size and a car, you'll compute its size in the image, storage, and detect it by color.

✎Q1 — Projection

Given

  • f = 8 mm
  • car height Y = 1.5 m
  • distance to car Z = 20 m
  • sensor 5.6 mm / 1920 px

Find

  • image height y (in mm)
  • then in pixels
✔Answer — Q1
Step 1y=ZfY​=200008×1500​=0.6 mm
Step 2pixels=0.6/5.6×1920≈206 px
∴ The car is ~206 px tall in the image
✎Q2 — Storage

Given

  • 1920 × 1080
  • RGB, 8-bit / channel

Find

  • (a) uncompressed size in MB
  • (b) size if grayscale
✔Answer — Q2
(a)1920×1080×3=6,220,800 bytes≈6.2 MB
(b)÷3=2,073,600 bytes≈2.1 MB
∴ RGB is 3× larger than grayscale

That trade-off is why many CV pipelines work in grayscale.

💻Q3 — Code

Verify Q2 with code, then detect the car's color.

Pythonexercise.py
import cv2, numpy as np
img = np.full((1080, 1920, 3), (60, 60, 200), np.uint8)   # synthetic 1920×1080 BGR scene (red)
# TODO 1: print shape and compute size in MB
# TODO 2: convert BGR → HSV
# TODO 3: build a mask for a red car (hue range)
🎯

Expected: shape printed, size matches Q2, red mask isolates the car

✔Answer — Q3
Pythonsolution.py
print(img.shape)        # (1080, 1920, 3)
size_mb = img.size / 1e6  # ≈ 6.2
hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2HSV)
mask = cv2.inRange(hsv, (0,100,100), (10,255,255))
cv2_imshow(mask)
